lesson.title: H(jw): The Single Expression That Describes an Entire Filter
lesson.summary: A transfer function packages a circuit's complete input to output behavior, magnitude and phase at every frequency, into one compact ratio of impedances.
lesson.body:
AC Circuit Analysis gives you the tools to solve for voltages and currents once every component is represented by its Impedance, a complex number that folds resistance and reactance together into a single quantity you can manipulate with the same algebra used for resistor networks. A transfer function takes that idea one step further: instead of solving for one particular output at one particular frequency, it expresses the ratio of output to input as a function of frequency itself, written H(jw), where j is the imaginary unit and w is angular frequency.

The classic example is a resistor capacitor low pass filter, with the output taken across the capacitor. Using the impedance of a capacitor, 1/(jwC), and treating the pair as a voltage divider, the transfer function works out to H(jw) = Zc / (R + Zc) = (1/(jwC)) / (R + 1/(jwC)). Multiplying numerator and denominator by jwC clears the fractions and gives the standard compact form H(jw) = 1 / (1 + jwRC). Everything about how this filter behaves at every possible frequency is compressed into that one expression.

Here is a fully worked numeric example. Let R = 1000 ohms and C = 1 microfarad, so RC = (1000)(0.000001) = 0.001 seconds. Evaluate the transfer function at w = 1000 rad/s. First compute wRC = (1000)(0.001) = 1, so H(jw) = 1 / (1 + j1). To get the magnitude, use the standard rule for a complex number a + jb, magnitude equals square root of (a squared + b squared), applied to the denominator: the denominator 1 + j1 has magnitude square root of (1 squared + 1 squared) = square root of 2 = 1.41421, and since the numerator is 1, the overall magnitude is |H| = 1 / 1.41421 = 0.7071. The phase angle of the denominator is arctan(1/1) = 45 degrees, and since the numerator contributes no phase, the overall phase of H is the negative of that, angle H = -45 degrees.

That specific frequency, w = 1000 rad/s, is not a random choice, it is the corner frequency of this particular RC network, the frequency at which wRC = 1. At exactly this point the output magnitude has dropped to 0.7071 of its low frequency value and the phase has shifted by exactly half of its maximum possible 90 degree shift. Both of those numbers, 0.7071 and 45 degrees, will reappear as defining landmarks once Frequency Response, Phase Response, and Magnitude Response are examined in detail using this exact same filter.

The power of writing H(jw) once and for all is that you never have to redo the impedance algebra for a new frequency, you simply substitute a different value of w into the same formula. This is what makes the transfer function the central object of AC circuit design: one expression, derived one time from Impedance, that predicts a circuit's complete behavior across the entire frequency spectrum, for any input frequency an engineer might care to check.
